steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Affected programs" section of a Wikipedia article on the A20 line: which DOS-era programs and tricks depended on the 8086 address wraparound, and how later DOS versions and boot loaders dealt with it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- DOS CALL 5 entry point and why it needs the wraparound
- A20 state and HMA workaround in newer DOS
- Programs using CALL 5
- Segment-sharing trick by BIOS/DOS programmers
- Failures once DOS loaded high; loader fixes, LOADFIX/MEMMAX
- Pascal, MASM, Spacemaker, EXEPACK; third-party fixes
- Modern boot loaders

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- CALL 5 (since 1980)
  - wrap used internally by 86-DOS and MS-DOS for DOS CALL 5 entry point at offset +5 to +9 in Program Segment Prefix (PSP)
  - emulates CP/M-80-style CALL 5 BDOS API entry at +5 to +7; PSP partially resembles CP/M-80 zero page
  - used by programs machine-translated from CP/M-80 via assembly language translators, e.g. Seattle Computer Products' TRANS86
  - handler at physical address 0x000000C0: overlaps four bytes of INT 30h entry and first byte of INT 31h in x86 real mode interrupt vector table
  - CP/M-80 loaded OS right above application memory, so 8080/Z80 16-bit target address at zero page +6 to +7 also = size of first memory segment
  - DOS with 8086 segment:offset: far call entry offset must match segment size (0xFEF0), stored at PSP +6 to +7, overlapping parts of CALL 5
  - only solution: segment value that + 0xFEF0 = 0x001000C0, wraps on 8086 to 0x000000C0
- A20 / HMA
  - A20 must be disabled for wraparound, so DOS programs using interface work
  - newer DOS relocating into HMA: copy of entry point at FFFF:00D0 in HMA (again physical 0x001000C0), works regardless of A20
- Programs using CALL 5
  - DOS version of Small-C compiler
  - SPELL utility in Microsoft's Word 3.0 (1987)
  - Sun Microsystems' PC-NFS (1993) needs CALL 5 fix-up
- Segment trick (to save program space)
  - BIOS/DOS programmers: one segment for program data (F800:0000 to F800:7FFF -> physical 0x000F8000–0x000FFFFF) and I/O data like keyboard buffer in first memory segment (F800:8000 to F800:FFFF -> 0x00000000 to 0x00007FFF)
  - works as long as code not executed in low memory (first 64 KB of RAM); always true in older DOS without load-high
- Failures
  - DOS kernel relocated higher -> low memory available to programs -> wraparound-dependent programs fail
  - newer DOS executable loaders detect common affected programs: patch on-the-fly for low memory, or load above first 64 KB
  - undetected programs: LOADFIX or MEMMAX -L force load above first 64 KB
- Tools using the trick
  - IBM/Microsoft Pascal and programs compiled with it, incl. Microsoft's MASM
  - executable compressors: Realia's Spacemaker (Robert B. K. Dewar, 1982; used to compress early Norton Utilities)
  - Microsoft's EXEPACK (Reuben Borman, 1985); /E[XEPACK] option in Microsoft's LINK 3.02 and higher
  - EXEPACK'd programs: "Packed file is corrupt" error
  - third-party utilities: replace uncompression routine(s) by restubbing, or expand/restore original file
- Boot loaders
  - modern Legacy BIOS boot loaders (GNU GRUB) use A20 line
  - UEFI boot loaders: 32-bit protected mode or 64-bit long mode

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Since 1980, 86-DOS and MS-DOS used the address wrap internally to implement the DOS CALL 5 entry point at offset +5 to +9 in the Program Segment Prefix (PSP) (the PSP partially resembles CP/M-80's zero page). This entry point emulates the CP/M-80-style CALL 5 BDOS API entry point, which was at offset +5 to +7. This was used in particular by programs that were machine-translated from CP/M-80 with assembly language translators, like TRANS86 from Seattle Computer Products. The CALL 5 handler that this entry point refers to is at the physical address 0x000000C0 of the machine (so it overlaps the four bytes of the interrupt service routine entry point reserved for INT 30h and also the first byte of INT 31h in the x86 real mode interrupt vector table). But because of the design of CP/M-80, which loaded the operating system right above the memory available for the application program to run in, the 8080/Z80 16-bit target address stored at offset +6 to +7 in the zero page could also be deliberately interpreted as the size of the first memory segment. To emulate this in DOS with its 8086 segment:offset addressing scheme, the 16-bit offset of the far call entry point had to match this segment size (i.e. 0xFEF0), which is stored at offset +6 to +7 in the PSP and overlaps parts of the CALL 5. The only way to make these requirements fit together was to choose a segment value that gives an address of 0x001000C0 when it is added to 0xFEF0, and on an 8086 this wraps around to 0x000000C0.

A20 had to be disabled so that the wraparound occurs and DOS programs that use this interface work. Newer DOS versions that can relocate parts of themselves into the HMA typically make a copy of the entry point at FFFF:00D0 in the HMA (which again resolves to physical 0x001000C0), so the interface can work no matter what the state of A20 is.

One program that is known to use the CALL 5 interface is the DOS version of the Small-C compiler. The SPELL utility in Microsoft's Word 3.0 (1987) is also one of the programs that depend on the CALL 5 interface being set up correspondingly. Sun Microsystems' PC-NFS (1993) also requires the CALL 5 fix-up.

- trick to save program space: one segment for program data (F800:0000 to F800:7FFF -> 0x000F8000–0x000FFFFF) and I/O data like keyboard buffer in first segment (F800:8000 to F800:FFFF -> 0x00000000 to 0x00007FFF)
- works unless code runs in low memory (first 64 KB); always true in older DOS without load-high
- DOS kernel moved high -> programs fail; newer loaders patch on-the-fly or load above first 64 KB; LOADFIX / MEMMAX -L otherwise
- IBM/Microsoft Pascal + compiled programs, MASM; Realia's Spacemaker (Robert B. K. Dewar, 1982, early Norton Utilities); EXEPACK (Reuben Borman, 1985), /E[XEPACK] in LINK 3.02+; "Packed file is corrupt"
- third-party utilities: restubbing or expand/restore
- Legacy BIOS boot loaders (GNU GRUB) use A20; UEFI uses 32-bit protected / 64-bit long mode

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Since 1980, 86-DOS and MS-DOS used the address wrap internally to implement the DOS CALL 5 entry point at offset +5 to +9 in the Program Segment Prefix (PSP) (the PSP partially resembles CP/M-80's zero page). This entry point emulates the CP/M-80-style CALL 5 BDOS API entry point, which was at offset +5 to +7. This was used in particular by programs that were machine-translated from CP/M-80 with assembly language translators, like TRANS86 from Seattle Computer Products. The CALL 5 handler that this entry point refers to is at the physical address 0x000000C0 of the machine (so it overlaps the four bytes of the interrupt service routine entry point reserved for INT 30h and also the first byte of INT 31h in the x86 real mode interrupt vector table). But because of the design of CP/M-80, which loaded the operating system right above the memory available for the application program to run in, the 8080/Z80 16-bit target address stored at offset +6 to +7 in the zero page could also be deliberately interpreted as the size of the first memory segment. To emulate this in DOS with its 8086 segment:offset addressing scheme, the 16-bit offset of the far call entry point had to match this segment size (i.e. 0xFEF0), which is stored at offset +6 to +7 in the PSP and overlaps parts of the CALL 5. The only way to make these requirements fit together was to choose a segment value that gives an address of 0x001000C0 when it is added to 0xFEF0, and on an 8086 this wraps around to 0x000000C0.

A20 had to be disabled so that the wraparound occurs and DOS programs that use this interface work. Newer DOS versions that can relocate parts of themselves into the HMA typically make a copy of the entry point at FFFF:00D0 in the HMA (which again resolves to physical 0x001000C0), so the interface can work no matter what the state of A20 is.

One program that is known to use the CALL 5 interface is the DOS version of the Small-C compiler. The SPELL utility in Microsoft's Word 3.0 (1987) is also one of the programs that depend on the CALL 5 interface being set up correspondingly. Sun Microsystems' PC-NFS (1993) also requires the CALL 5 fix-up.

Also, some BIOS and DOS programmers used a trick to save program space. For example, they had one segment that has access to program data (such as from F800:0000 to F800:7FFF, which points to the physical addresses 0x000F8000–0x000FFFFF) and also to the I/O data (such as the keyboard buffer) that was in the first memory segment (with addresses F800:8000 to F800:FFFF pointing to the physical addresses 0x00000000 to 0x00007FFF).

This trick works as long as the code is not executed in low memory, which is the first 64 KB of RAM. This condition was always true in older DOS versions that had no load-high capabilities.

When the DOS kernel was relocated into higher memory areas, low memory became more and more available for programs, and this made the programs that depend on the wraparound fail. The executable loaders in newer versions of DOS try to detect some common types of affected programs and then either patch them on-the-fly so they also work in low memory or load them above the first 64 KB before passing execution on to them. For programs that are not detected automatically, LOADFIX or MEMMAX -L can be used to force them to be loaded above the first 64 KB.

IBM/Microsoft Pascal itself used the trick, and so did programs compiled with it, including Microsoft's MASM. Other commonly used development utilities that used it were executable compressors like Realia's Spacemaker (Robert B. K. Dewar wrote it in 1982 and it was used to compress early versions of the Norton Utilities) and Microsoft's EXEPACK (Reuben Borman wrote it in 1985), and also the equivalent /E[XEPACK] option in Microsoft's LINK 3.02 and higher. Programs that were processed with EXEPACK would display a "Packed file is corrupt" error message.

There are various third-party utilities to modify compressed executables, either by replacing the problematic uncompression routine(s) through restubbing, or by trying to expand and restore the original file.

Modern Legacy BIOS boot loaders (such as GNU GRUB) use the A20 line. UEFI boot loaders use 32-bit protected mode or 64-bit long mode.
